questions.prompt: In financial return prediction, what does an out-of-sample R² of roughly 0.01–0.02 (1–2% of variance explained) generally indicate, per Lesson 1?
options: A genuinely strong result, not a failure, given markets' structurally low signal-to-noise ratio
A model performing barely above random guessing that should be discarded
Clear evidence of a coding bug, since real signal should explain far more variance than that
A result that is typical for image classification models, not for return-prediction models
An R² value that is mathematically impossible for a well-specified regression
Evidence the model is underfitting and needs many more engineered features
questions.explain: In an efficient (or close to efficient) market, easily exploitable patterns get traded away quickly, so what's left for a model to find is faint by nature — the lesson states a model explaining 1–2% of next-period return variance is often considered strong, while anything above roughly 5% out-of-sample should raise suspicion of leakage. That's the opposite of how R² reads in domains like image classification.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B applies the intuition from other ML domains, where 1–2% of variance explained would indeed look like a barely-functioning model. But Lesson 1 is explicit that this intuition doesn't transfer to finance: because real financial signal is so faint to begin with, a tiny R² can be a genuinely strong, real result rather than a sign of failure.

questions.prompt: A researcher's brand-new return-prediction model, tested on real historical market data for the first time, reports an out-of-sample R² of 0.40. What should the researcher conclude, per Lesson 1?
options: The far more likely explanation is a bug — look-ahead bias, a leaked label, or data misalignment — not a genuine breakthrough
The model has found a strong, reliable trading signal and should be deployed immediately
This is a normal, expected result for financial data once enough engineered features are used
The R² metric simply doesn't apply to financial return prediction, so the number is meaningless
questions.explain: Lesson 1 frames this explicitly as a calibration exercise: if a first model on real return data reports an R² of 0.4, the far more likely explanation is a bug like look-ahead bias, a leaked label, or data misalignment — not a breakthrough. A result that far outside the normal 1–2% range should trigger suspicion, not celebration.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about look-ahead bias and survivorship bias, per Lesson 2.
options: Look-ahead bias happens when a backtest uses information that was not actually knowable at that point in time
Survivorship bias happens when the universe of tested assets only includes companies, funds, or coins that still exist today, excluding failures and delistings
Survivorship bias tends to make backtest results look worse than they would have looked in live trading
Using an index's current constituent list to test a strategy ten years in the past is an example of look-ahead bias
Both biases are eliminated automatically just by using a time-ordered split instead of shuffled k-fold cross-validation
questions.explain: Look-ahead bias is using information that wasn't actually available at that point in time — exactly what happens when a backtest uses a restated earnings figure before its restatement, or today's index constituents a decade in the past. Survivorship bias is testing only on assets that still exist today, which flatters results rather than worsening them, since the excluded failures are the ones most likely to have had a real problem the strategy should have caught. Neither bias is about row ordering, so a time-ordered split does nothing to fix either one.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a real predictive signal that weakens or disappears over time as more market participants discover and trade on it is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 1 defines alpha decay as exactly this: even a genuine, working signal tends to decay once enough market participants discover and trade on it — the signal doesn't just get noisy, it can quietly stop existing.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of computing and applying uniqueness-based sample weights in the correct order, per Lesson 4.
items: Determine each label's window boundaries (start and end bar) from the triple-barrier labeling process
Compute concurrency: for every bar, count how many labels' windows cover it
Compute each label's average uniqueness as the mean of 1 divided by concurrency across its own window
Pass the resulting per-label weights into the model's `sample_weight` argument during `.fit()`
questions.explain: Lesson 4 builds this chain in order: a label's window first has to be known before concurrency can be computed across bars, concurrency then feeds directly into the average-uniqueness calculation for each label, and only once those weights exist can they be handed to `sample_weight` in scikit-learn's, XGBoost's, or LightGBM's `.fit()` — so overlapping, non-unique labels don't dominate training the way independent observations would.

questions.prompt: A researcher has a financial factor set with several highly correlated momentum variants (5-day, 10-day, and 20-day momentum, which largely measure overlapping information) and fits a Lasso model. What is the most likely practical consequence, per Lesson 5?
options: Lasso will arbitrarily pick one of the correlated momentum variants and zero out the rest, which can make the selected features unstable across retrainings
Lasso will average the correlated features together into a single new feature automatically
Lasso will refuse to fit, since it cannot handle any correlated features at all
Lasso will keep all correlated features with roughly equal, nonzero coefficients, the same way Ridge would
questions.explain: Lesson 5 states this as Lasso's specific pitfall: with strongly correlated features, Lasso tends to arbitrarily pick one of a correlated group and zero out the rest, which can make the selected features unstable across retrainings — a risk Ridge doesn't have, since Ridge shrinks all coefficients together rather than zeroing most of them out.

questions.code:
xgb_model = XGBRegressor(
    n_estimators=1000,
    learning_rate=0.02,
    max_depth=3,
    subsample=0.7,
    colsample_bytree=0.7,
    reg_alpha=0.1,
    reg_lambda=1.0,
    early_stopping_rounds=50,
    eval_metric="rmse",
    random_state=0,
)
questions.prompt: A researcher removes `early_stopping_rounds` from this XGBoost setup and instead trains all 1,000 rounds unconditionally. The training curve keeps improving round after round, but validation performance gets steadily worse past a certain point. What does this indicate, and what's the direct fix per Lesson 7?
options: The model is fitting the noise left in the residuals round after round; using `early_stopping_rounds` to halt once validation error stops improving is the direct fix
The learning rate is too small and should be increased to speed up convergence instead
This divergence between training and validation curves is expected and harmless behavior for any boosted model
The fix is to switch from XGBoost to a random forest, since boosting cannot be regularized at all
questions.explain: Each boosting round fits a new tree to the ensemble's residual errors so far, which keeps chasing whatever pattern is left — including noise — if allowed to run too long. Lesson 7 describes exactly this symptom (training keeps improving while validation gets worse) as under-regularized boosting on low-signal data, and early stopping is the direct fix: it lets validation error decide how many rounds are actually useful instead of guessing at `n_estimators`.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about decision trees and random forests, per Lesson 6.
options: An unconstrained single decision tree can grow until each leaf has just one or two examples, memorizing noise along with real signal
A random forest fits many trees, each on a bootstrap-resampled subset of rows and a random subset of features per split, then averages their predictions
Random forests eliminate the need to constrain `max_depth` or `min_samples_leaf`, since averaging alone makes unlimited tree depth safe
Averaging many trees that each overfit to different noise cancels out a lot of that noise while real, shared signal survives the averaging
`.feature_importances_` is described in the lesson as a final, unbiased answer for which features actually matter
questions.explain: A single unconstrained tree can grow to near-perfect memorization of training data, including its noise. Random forests average many trees fit on bootstrapped rows and random feature subsets, which cancels idiosyncratic noise while real shared signal survives. But the lesson is explicit that constraining `max_depth`/`min_samples_leaf` still matters even with that averaging — it doesn't make unlimited depth safe — and `.feature_importances_` is explicitly called a rough first look with real limitations, not a final answer.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ Net blends Lasso's L1 penalty and Ridge's L2 penalty using a mixing parameter (`l1_ratio`), gaining some of Lasso's feature selection while keeping more of Ridge's stability under collinearity.
questions.explain: Lesson 5 describes Elastic Net as exactly this practical middle ground — a weighted blend of the L1 and L2 penalties, often the most practical choice for real financial factor sets where some features are correlated and some are likely irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Match each term from Chapter 2 to what it actually does.
right: Halts boosting once validation error stops improving for a set number of rounds
An L2 weight-decay penalty discouraging the network from growing large weights to fit noise
Fixed-weight averaging of multiple base models' predictions
Trains a meta-model on base models' out-of-fold predictions to learn how to combine them
questions.explain: VotingRegressor does fixed-weight averaging of base models (Lesson 9). StackingRegressor instead trains a meta-model on base models' out-of-fold predictions to learn how to combine them (Lesson 9). `early_stopping_rounds` halts XGBoost once validation error stops improving (Lesson 7). MLPRegressor's `alpha` is an L2 weight-decay penalty functioning much like Ridge's penalty (Lesson 8).

questions.prompt: Why does Hierarchical Risk Parity (HRP) avoid the instability that plagues Markowitz mean-variance optimization on correlated financial assets, per Lesson 13?
options: HRP never inverts the covariance matrix — it only ever compares the variance of one sub-cluster to another when allocating weight recursively
HRP uses a numerically more stable algorithm for inverting the covariance matrix than Markowitz does
HRP avoids instability by only ever investing in a single, lowest-volatility asset
HRP removes the need for a covariance matrix entirely and allocates weight using only price momentum
questions.explain: Markowitz's optimal weights come from a formula involving the inverse of the covariance matrix, which becomes numerically unstable when assets are highly correlated. HRP sidesteps the inversion entirely: tree clustering, quasi-diagonalization, and recursive bisection only ever compare the variance of one sub-cluster against another, so a noisy estimate in one corner of the matrix doesn't blow up the whole allocation the way an unstable matrix inverse can.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about using `GaussianMixture` versus `KMeans` for market-regime detection, per Lesson 10.
options: `GaussianMixture`'s `predict_proba` can express a day as a soft mix — e.g. 70% high-vol regime, 30% transitioning — rather than forcing one hard label
`KMeans` assumes spherical, equal-size clusters, while `GaussianMixture` with `covariance_type="full"` allows each regime its own shape and variance
`KMeans` is a genuine probabilistic model, while `GaussianMixture` only ever produces hard cluster labels
The "correct" number of market regimes is a fact directly discoverable from the data, with no modeling judgment involved
The elbow method and the silhouette score are mentioned as diagnostics to help choose the number of clusters
questions.explain: `GaussianMixture` is a genuine probabilistic model that gives soft, per-regime membership probabilities via `predict_proba`, and its `covariance_type="full"` lets each regime have its own shape instead of assuming spherical, equal-size clusters the way `KMeans` does — which is backwards from option C. Lesson 10 is also explicit that nothing in the data reveals the "true" number of clusters; it's a modeling choice guided by diagnostics like the elbow method and silhouette score, not a fact to be discovered.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the `contamination` parameter in `IsolationForest` and `EllipticEnvelope` sets your prior on what ________ of the data you expect to be anomalous, which directly sets the decision threshold.
questions.explain: Lesson 12 states this directly: `contamination` is your prior on what fraction of the data you expect to be anomalous, and it directly sets the decision threshold the model uses to flag outliers.

questions.prompt: Match each unsupervised-learning tool to what it actually does, per Chapter 3.
left: PCA's first principal component (PC1) on an equity returns panel
right: Informally called the "market factor" because it loads positively on nearly every asset
Learns a flexible boundary enclosing the dense region of "normal" data; anything outside is flagged
Lets you cluster using a domain-specific distance, like correlation distance, instead of being limited to Euclidean distance on raw features
Fits a single robust Gaussian ellipse to the data and flags points far from its center
questions.explain: `AgglomerativeClustering` with a precomputed metric lets you plug in a domain-specific distance like correlation distance (Lesson 10). PCA's PC1 on a broad equity panel almost always loads positively across nearly every asset, earning the informal name "market factor" (Lesson 11). `OneClassSVM` learns a flexible enclosing boundary (Lesson 12). `EllipticEnvelope` fits a single robust Gaussian ellipse and flags points far from its center (Lesson 12).

questions.prompt: What is the core difference between what purging and embargoing each remove from the training set in purged and embargoed cross-validation?
options: Purging removes training rows whose label window overlaps the test span (usually just before it); embargoing removes a further buffer of training rows positioned immediately after the test span, regardless of label overlap
Purging removes rows positioned after the test set; embargoing removes rows whose labels overlap the test set — the opposite pairing
Purging and embargoing both remove exactly the same rows; they are simply two names for the identical operation
Purging removes an entire asset from the dataset; embargoing removes an entire calendar year from the dataset
Purging applies only inside `KFold`; embargoing applies only inside `TimeSeriesSplit`, and the two are never combined in one splitter
Embargoing removes training rows whose labels overlap the test span; purging guards against serial correlation after the test span — the opposite pairing
questions.explain: Lesson 15 defines the two fixes for two separate leaks: purging removes training observations whose label window overlaps the test set's time span (typically rows just before the test block, filtered by where each label actually resolves), while embargoing separately removes a buffer of rows immediately after the test block, filtered only by raw position, as a precaution against serial correlation and rolling-window feature leakage — not because of any label overlap.
questions.distractorExplain: Option F describes the same two mechanisms but swaps which name goes with which job — it's purging that's tied to label-window overlap (handled via `label_end`, usually on the side before the test block), and embargoing that's the flat positional buffer guarding against serial correlation after the test block. Getting the two names backwards is exactly the mistake this lesson's terminology is designed to prevent.

questions.code:
def split(self, X, y=None, groups=None):
    for test_start, test_stop in self._test_ranges(n):
        test_idx = indices[test_start:test_stop]
        before = indices[indices < test_start]
        after = indices[indices >= test_stop]
        before = before[self.label_end[before] < test_start]   # PURGE
        after = after[after >= test_stop + embargo]              # EMBARGO
        train_idx = np.concatenate([before, after])
        yield train_idx, test_idx
questions.prompt: Put these steps of `PurgedKFold.split()` in the order they actually execute, per Lesson 15.
items: Determine the current fold's test-set start and stop boundaries
From rows before the test fold, purge any whose label window reaches into the test span (label_end >= test_start)
From rows after the test fold, embargo a further buffer of rows immediately following the test span, regardless of their own label window
Concatenate the surviving before- and after-rows into the final training set yielded for this fold
questions.explain: `PurgedKFold` first fixes the test span's boundaries for the current fold, then applies two separate filters: the `before` branch is purging, filtered by where each label actually resolves (`label_end`); the `after` branch is embargoing, filtered purely by position with no reference to `label_end` at all. Only after both filters run are the surviving rows concatenated into the training set that gets yielded.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of computing the Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) via combinatorially symmetric cross-validation in the correct order, per Lesson 18.
items: Split the strategy's performance history into several subsamples
Form every possible way to combine half of the subsamples into an in-sample set and the other half into an out-of-sample set
For each such combination, pick the configuration that performed best in-sample
Check whether that in-sample winner ranks above or below the median out-of-sample performer
Compute PBO as the fraction of combinations where the in-sample winner was a below-median out-of-sample performer
questions.explain: Lesson 18 builds PBO in exactly this order: the performance history is split into subsamples first, every symmetric in-sample/out-of-sample combination of those subsamples is formed, the in-sample-best configuration is identified for each combination, its out-of-sample rank is checked against the median, and PBO is finally reported as the fraction of combinations where that in-sample winner turned out to be a below-median out-of-sample performer.

questions.prompt: A researcher runs a single purged walk-forward validation and gets a Sharpe ratio of 1.8. A colleague suggests running Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation (CPCV) instead before trusting that number. Why, per Lesson 16?
options: A single walk-forward path is only one sample from the space of how the strategy could have played out; CPCV produces a distribution of Sharpe ratios across many held-out combinations, revealing whether the edge is consistent or depends on which slice of history was tested
CPCV is required because `TimeSeriesSplit` cannot be purged or embargoed at all
CPCV will always produce a higher Sharpe ratio than a single walk-forward split, so it should be preferred for that reason alone
CPCV eliminates the need for an embargo, since testing every combination of groups already prevents any leakage
questions.explain: Lesson 16 makes the point directly: even a scrupulously leak-free single backtest path is still just one sample from the space of how the strategy could have played out. CPCV holds out every combination of k groups out of N, each purged and embargoed, producing a distribution of Sharpe ratios whose spread tells you whether the apparent edge is consistent across different slices of history or just got lucky on the one path originally tested.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Probabilistic Sharpe Ratio (PSR) and the Deflated Sharpe Ratio (DSR), per Lesson 17.
options: PSR accounts for the return distribution's skewness and kurtosis, not just its mean and standard deviation
DSR evaluates PSR against a benchmark of zero — the same benchmark PSR itself uses
The benchmark DSR uses rises with both the number of trials and how much the trials' Sharpe ratios vary from each other
A DSR near 0.5 or below suggests the headline Sharpe ratio is consistent with pure multiple-testing luck rather than genuine skill
The expected maximum Sharpe ratio among many zero-skill trials is centered at zero regardless of how many trials were run
questions.explain: PSR's confidence calculation already reflects sample length, skewness, and kurtosis. DSR is PSR evaluated against the expected maximum Sharpe ratio from N zero-skill trials — not zero — and that benchmark rises with both the number of trials and their dispersion, which is exactly why a DSR near or below 0.5 signals the headline Sharpe looks like pure multiple-testing luck. The expected maximum of many zero-skill draws drifts upward as more trials are run; it is not centered at zero.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Probability of Backtest ________ (PBO) is the fraction of in-sample/out-of-sample combinations, from combinatorially symmetric cross-validation, where the in-sample-best configuration turns out to be a below-median out-of-sample performer.
questions.explain: Lesson 18 defines PBO exactly this way — a direct measure of how often picking the best in-sample configuration leads to a mediocre or bad out-of-sample result, built on a CPCV-like symmetric splitting of the performance history.

questions.prompt: A random forest's `.feature_importances_` (MDI) ranks `momentum_5d` as the single most important feature. When the researcher instead runs permutation importance on a held-out purged fold, `momentum_5d` contributes almost nothing to out-of-sample performance. What does this discrepancy most likely indicate, per Lesson 19?
options: The model may be overfitting to that feature in-sample, since MDI is computed in-sample and can be inflated by correlated/substitute features, while permutation importance is measured out-of-sample against real predictive performance
Permutation importance is broken and should be disregarded in favor of MDI in this case
`momentum_5d` must be a categorical feature, which MDI cannot score correctly
The discrepancy proves the model has zero predictive power of any kind
questions.explain: Lesson 19 flags exactly this pattern as a red flag: MDI is computed in-sample and can look important purely because the model overfit to noise, and it's also biased toward correlated/substitute features, which are common in finance. Permutation importance is measured out-of-sample by actually breaking the feature's signal, so when the two disagree this sharply, the lesson's recommended read is that the model may be overfitting to that feature in-sample.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), per Lesson 20.
options: For any individual prediction, SHAP values for every feature add up exactly to (prediction − baseline)
`TreeExplainer` computes Shapley values efficiently and exactly for tree-based models like random forests and XGBoost
Shapley values are computed by averaging a feature's marginal contribution over every possible ordering in which features could be added
SHAP can only ever produce one overall importance ranking for a whole dataset, the same as permutation importance, with no per-prediction detail
A feature whose SHAP values scatter on both sides regardless of its own level is a hint the model may be picking up noise rather than a real relationship
questions.explain: SHAP values for a prediction add up exactly to (prediction − baseline), `TreeExplainer` computes them efficiently and exactly for tree models, and a Shapley value is the average marginal contribution across every possible feature-ordering — all stated directly in Lesson 20. The lesson explicitly contrasts SHAP against single-ranking methods: it goes further by attributing each individual prediction to its features, so option D is backwards.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the Information Coefficient (IC) is the rank correlation (typically ________) between a signal's predicted values and the actual forward returns, computed period by period.
questions.explain: Lesson 21 defines IC as the rank correlation — typically Spearman's — between predicted values and actual forward returns, computed period by period, and tracked across rolling windows to check whether a signal's edge is stable or decaying.

questions.prompt: A researcher builds a 20-day sequence window for an LSTM, stepping the window forward one day at a time, then validates using an otherwise-correct purged walk-forward split. Why might this still leak information, per Lesson 22?
options: Consecutive training windows overlap by 19 out of 20 days, which is the same overlapping-outcome leakage problem from Chapters 1 and 4, except it now applies to every input window rather than just the label horizon, and a purge computed only around the label can miss it
LSTMs are mathematically incapable of being validated with any purged cross-validation scheme
This is not actually a leakage risk, since stepping forward one day at a time is the standard, leak-free way to build a sequence
The leak only happens if the sequence window exceeds 252 trading days
questions.explain: Lesson 22 is explicit that sequence models make the overlapping-window problem worse, not better: each training example is itself a window of rows, and stepping it forward one day at a time means consecutive examples share nearly their entire input window — the same overlapping-labels problem from Chapter 1/4's purging logic, now baked into how the sequences were constructed rather than just how they were split, which makes it easy to overlook.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about financial NLP, per Lesson 23.
options: General-purpose sentiment dictionaries can misclassify ordinary financial vocabulary, like reading "liability" or "tax" as negative even in routine, neutral filing language
The Loughran-McDonald lexicon was built from actual financial disclosures specifically to correct this kind of misclassification
Bag-of-words sentiment scoring accounts for word order and context, the same way a transformer-based model does
Using a filing's content but timestamping the resulting feature to the fiscal period it covers, rather than its actual release date, hands the model information before it existed in the real world
Even with correct timing and a properly fine-tuned model, text-derived sentiment signals tend to be noisy
questions.explain: Lesson 23 states that general sentiment dictionaries misread routine financial vocabulary, the Loughran-McDonald lexicon exists specifically to fix that, mistimed filing features leak future information the same way other timing leaks do, and even correctly-timed, well-built sentiment signals remain noisy. Bag-of-words is the opposite of context-aware — it throws away word order and context entirely, which is precisely the limitation transformer-based models like FinBERT were built to address.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: trading on material non-public information, abbreviated ________, is illegal regardless of how the information was obtained.
questions.explain: Lesson 24 defines MNPI as information that would move a security's price if disclosed and isn't available to the public, and states plainly that trading on it is illegal, full stop, regardless of how it was obtained — which is why every new alternative-data source needs a compliance review before it reaches a model.

questions.prompt: Match each reinforcement-learning term to what it actually is, per Lesson 25.
right: Learns the mapping from state to action directly, without first learning a value function
What the agent observes before acting: market features, price history, and its own portfolio
The feedback signal received after acting, typically risk-adjusted profit-and-loss
Learns an expected-value function over state-action pairs and acts by choosing the highest-value action
questions.explain: The state is what the agent observes before acting — market features, price history, and its own portfolio. The reward is the feedback signal received afterward, typically risk-adjusted P&L. Q-learning/DQN learns an expected-value function over state-action pairs and picks the highest-value action. Policy-gradient methods skip the value function and learn the state-to-action mapping directly.

questions.prompt: Put these four decisions of locking in a validation plan before training anything in the correct order, per Lesson 26.
items: Decide the cross-validation scheme: purged and embargoed walk-forward CV at minimum, or CPCV if compute allows
Decide the purge and embargo windows based on the label's own time horizon
Decide the evaluation metric up front: out-of-sample Information Coefficient plus a risk-adjusted return metric, not just raw accuracy
Decide how uncertainty will be reported: a distribution across folds, and the deflated Sharpe ratio if more than one configuration is tried
questions.explain: Lesson 26 lays out these four decisions as a required pre-commitment, in this order: first fix the CV scheme itself, then size the purge/embargo windows around the label's own horizon, then fix the evaluation metric, and finally decide how uncertainty itself will be reported — all four written down before a single model is fit, which is what separates honest research from fitting the validation scheme to a result you already liked.

questions.prompt: In the Lesson 27 worked capstone example, a fresh `fold_model` is instantiated and fit separately inside every fold of the validation loop, rather than fitting one model once on the full dataset beforehand. Why does this matter?
options: Fitting once on the full dataset and then "validating" afterward is exactly the bolted-on-after-the-fact mistake the capstone brief warns against; each fold needs its own freshly-trained model so that fold's test rows were never seen during that fold's own training
XGBoost models cannot be re-instantiated more than once per Python session
Fitting inside each fold is purely a performance optimization with no effect on the validity of the result
A full-dataset fit would have produced results identical to fitting per fold, so the distinction is cosmetic
questions.explain: Lesson 27 states this directly: fitting once on everything and then validating afterward is exactly the bolted-on-after-the-fact mistake Lesson 26 warned against. Fitting a fresh model inside each fold guarantees that fold's held-out test rows were never part of that model's own training data — the entire point of purged walk-forward validation.

questions.prompt: Match each element of a capstone write-up to what a reviewer is actually checking for, per Lesson 28.
left: Timestamping of every feature and label
right: Whether it's purged and embargoed walk-forward CV (or something stronger), not a random k-fold that ignores time order
Whether only information actually available at that point in time was used, avoiding look-ahead bias
Whether it's a skeptical, deflated estimate across folds rather than a single flattering number
Whether a good-looking aggregate metric was accepted at face value or actually checked for robustness
questions.explain: Lesson 28 lists five things a reviewer is actually checking for, and these four map directly: careful timestamping is checked against look-ahead bias, the CV method is checked against naive k-fold, the reported performance number is checked for whether it's a skeptical deflated estimate rather than one flattering figure, and feature importance/stability is checked for whether it was actually examined rather than taken on faith.
